However, methods like Sylber and SyllableLM rely on intricate multi-stage training pipelines. We propose ZeroSyl, a simple training-free method to extract syllable boundaries and embeddings directly from a frozen WavLM model. Using L2 norms of features in WavLM's intermediate layers, ZeroSyl achieves competitive syllable segmentation performance. The resulting segments are mean-pooled, discretized using K-means, and used to train a language model. ZeroSyl outperforms prior syllabic tokenizers across lexical, syntactic, and narrative benchmarks. Scaling experiments show that while finer-grained units are beneficial for lexical tasks, our discovered syllabic units exhibit better scaling behavior for syntactic modeling.

items.title: Towards Data-free and Training-free Compression for Speech Foundation Models Using Parameter Clustering
items.abstract: This paper presents a novel data-free and training-free compression approach for speech foundation models using channel-wise clustering via k-means. More fine-grained, mixed sparsity pruning by layer-level varying number of parameter clusters is also explored. Experiments conducted on the LibriSpeech dataset suggest that when operating with pruning sparsity of 50% on HuBERT-large, consistent WER reductions of 27.73%/18.61% absolute (34.37%/21.91% relative) over the magnitude-based pruning were obtained on the test-clean and test-other subsets before fine-tuning and 0.19%/0.79% absolute (3.36%/4.62% relative) after fine-tuning with only 3 epochs. Similar WER reductions of 2.86%/5.02% absolute (59.21%/55.29% relative) were observed against magnitude-based pruning on Whisper-large-v3 at 10% sparsity, all with no significant WER increase relative to the uncompressed baseline.

items.title: OnDA: On-device Channel Pruning for Efficient Personalized Keyword Spotting
items.abstract: Always-on keyword spotting (KWS) demands on-device adaptation to cope with user- and environment-specific distribution shifts under tight latency and energy budgets. This paper proposes, for the first time, coupling weight adaptation (i.e., on-device training) with architectural adaptation, in the form of online structured channel pruning, for personalized on-device KWS. Starting from a state-of-the-art self-learning personalized KWS pipeline, we compare data-agnostic and data-aware pruning criteria applied on in-field pseudo-labelled user data. On the HeySnips and HeySnapdragon datasets, we achieve up to 9.63× model-size compression with respect to unpruned baselines at iso-task performance, measured as the accuracy at 0.5 false alarms per hour. When deploying our adaptation pipeline on a Jetson Orin Nano embedded GPU, we achieve up to 1.52×/1.57× and 1.64×/1.77× latency and energy-consumption improvements during online training/inference compared to weights-only adaptation.

items.title: Sub-Model Short-Term Memory Convolutions for Keyword Spotting Systems on Device
items.abstract: Keyword Spotting (KWS) is becoming increasingly important as voice-controlled devices grow more widespread. While voice interaction with smartphones and smart TVs is already common, deploying KWS on heavily resource-constrained edge devices such as wearables remains challenging. These systems must meet high accuracy requirements while operating under strict constraints on computational power, memory footprint, and real-time latency. In this work, we present an application of the STMC (Short-Term Memory Convolutions) framework to adapt a modular CNN model for online, LSTM-like inference. Our approach reduces power consumption and redundant computations while maintaining the stability and simplicity of training CNNs. We achieve up to 82% and 46% MCPS reduction compared to equivalently frequent standard CNN execution and vanilla STMC, respectively. The best configuration achieves 93.8% accuracy on the 11-class Google Speech Commands task and 97.1% on the same task with zero-padded data.

items.title: An Efficient vLLM-Based Inference Pipeline for Unified Audio Understanding and Generation
items.abstract: While Large Multimodal Models excel in comprehension, high-throughput inference engines lack native support for multimodal generation. This is severe in Speech Language Models, where generating multi-layered audio tokens via decoupled AR+NAR or synchronous Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) with delay-pattern interleaving conflicts with standard single-stream loops. We present a vLLM-based inference pipeline for unified speech understanding and generation. We extend autoregressive decoding to natively execute delay-pattern de-interleaving and coordinated multi-stream sampling, integrating an on-GPU acoustic decoder for end-to-end waveform synthesis. Crucially, we overcome the shared intuition that Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) halves throughput. By co-scheduling paired conditional and unconditional requests within a continuous batch, our CFG implementation sustains 80% of non-CFG throughput, absorbing dual-request and logit merging overheads. We open-source our framework1.

items.title: Audio-NSP: Data-Centric Semi-Autoregressive Generation for Large Audio-Language Models
items.abstract: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) suffer from high latency due to the autoregressive decoding of long audio sequences. We propose Audio-NSP (Next Sequence Prediction), a framework that activates semi-autoregressive parallel generation in pre-trained LALMs solely through data-centric Supervised Fine-Tuning. By restructuring training sequences with blockwise attention, Audio-NSP enables simultaneous multi-token prediction without architectural modifications. Crucially, applying this to audio reveals a decoding dilemma caused by the entropy gap between deterministic text and highly variable audio tokens. To resolve this, we introduce a modality-aware dynamic truncation strategy. It applies strict thresholds for text and lenient thresholds for audio, preventing degeneration into single-step decoding while preserving fidelity. Experiments show Audio-NSP achieves speedups of up to 3.42x while significantly outperforming Multi-Token Prediction baselines in quality preservation.

items.title: Improving streaming ASR with foundation models using emission policies
items.abstract: Speech Foundation Models (SFMs) have achieved state-of-the-art results in offline ASR, yet their application in streaming environments remains limited due to the performance degradation caused by restricted context. In this work, we propose a model-agnostic, training-free streaming pipeline designed to wrap around ASR models in a "black box" manner. Our approach integrates three key components: a sliding window audio buffer for incremental data ingestion, token-level timestamp management to eliminate redundant output, and text-only emission policies to govern output timing. We systematically evaluate several emission policies, assessing their impact on the latency-accuracy trade-off across three English datasets. Results show that our pipeline enables timestamp-producing SFMs like Parakeet and Canary to achieve near-offline transcription quality in real-time environments without requiring access to internal model tensors.

items.title: AdaTS: Adaptive Token Sampling for Efficient Speech Language Models
items.abstract: Speech Language Models (SLMs) have demonstrated strong speech understanding capabilities by incorporating speech tokens into large LMs (LLMs). However, most designs are i) token-intensive, as a large part of the LLM context is allotted to speech tokens, and ii) inefficient, as speech tokens are often temporally redundant, hindering SLMs’ capabilities to handle long-form tasks. To address both issues, we propose AdaTS, a dynamic sampling method that adaptively merges tokens where the speech signal is less informative. Our approach reduces the length of the speech signal seen by the LLM by 2× or more, with performance often better than standard downsampling across automatic speech recognition (ASR), speech question-answering (SQA), and speech translation (ST). Through an extensive empirical analysis, we show how SLMs using AdaTS retain strong speech understanding capabilities, while substantially reducing token redundancy and inference cost by 40%.

items.title: Merging the Knowledge of LLMs for Automatic Speech Recognition
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, trained on paired speech-text data, have been improved by leveraging language models (LMs) trained on text-only data. LM fusion methods such as shallow fusion and density ratio are well-established methods that incorporate external LMs during ASR decoding. However, they incur additional computational costs due to LM inference, which is particularly problematic for recent larger LMs. In this study, we propose incorporating external LMs via model merging. This method integrates the LMs directly into the parameters of an LLM-based ASR model, requiring no additional computational cost at inference. We formulate domain extension and transfer via arithmetic operations on LoRA parameters. Experimental evaluations were conducted for the domain adaptation of LLM-based ASR trained on CSJ and LibriSpeech. We show that our LM merging consistently improved the ASR performance in the target domains, without degrading inference speed or memory footprint.

items.title: Scaling few-shot spoken word classification with generative meta-continual learning
items.abstract: Few-shot spoken word classification has largely been developed for applications where a small number of classes is considered, and so the potential of larger-scale few-shot spoken word classification remains untapped. This paper investigates the potential of a spoken word classifier to sequentially learn to distinguish between 1 000 classes when it is given only five shots per class. We demonstrate that this scaling capability exists by training a model using the Generative Meta-Continual Learning (GeMCL) algorithm and comparing it to repeatedly trained or finetuned baselines. We find that GeMCL produces exceptionally stable performance, and although it does not always outperform a repeatedly fully-finetuned HuBERT model nor a frozen HuBERT model with a repeatedly trained classifier head, it produces comparable performance to the latter while adapting 2 000 times faster, having been trained on less than half of the data for two orders of magnitude less time.

items.title: SEA-MDD: Self-adapting Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis Models via Test-Time Training
items.abstract: Mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) assists second language (L2) learners in improving pronunciation. However, the substantial variability in learner proficiency and the diverse mispronunciation types hinder the development of reliable MDD systems. Large-scale annotation to cover all mispronunciations is prohibitively expensive. To address this data scarcity, we propose SEA-MDD, a SElf-Adapting MDD method that leverages Test-Time Training (TTT) to effectively adapt trained models to new speech samples. Specifically, we integrate multilayer perceptron (MLP)-based TTT modules into Transformer blocks of wav2vec 2.0. The parameters of TTT modules are updated during both training and test time via self-supervised learning. This design enables trained models to adjust dynamically to novel inputs, mitigating performance degradation commonly observed in prior MDD models when exposed to diverse speech distributions. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

items.title: Mixture-of-Accent-Adapters for Robust ASR: Injecting Accent Cues into Pretrained Whisper
items.abstract: Accented speech remains a key challenge for inclusive ASR, yet adapting large pretrained models often relies on costly full fine-tuning. Moreover, previous methods lack integration of accent-specific adapters, controlled encoder-level accent-cue injection, and multitask supervision for specialization regulation and gender information leakage mitigation. We propose Mixture-of-Accent-Adapters (MoAA), a novel adaptation framework for Whisper that enables on-demand specialization while defaulting to the frozen backbone when unnecessary. A pooled-state control bottleneck estimates accentedness, guiding accent-cue injection via weighted retrieval from a learnable soft accent codebook and routing lightweight accent-specialist adapters, while calibrating a gated blend with the backbone. An adversarial gender head reduces leakage, and reference-free hallucination suppression mitigates rare decoding artifacts. On AESRC benchmark, MoAA achieves 7.49% WER and 3.81% CER.

items.title: Contrastive Regularization for Accent-Robust ASR
items.abstract: ASR systems based on self-supervised acoustic pretraining and CTC fine-tuning achieve strong performance on native speech but remain sensitive to accent variability. We investigate supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) as a lightweight, accent-invariant auxiliary objective for CTC fine-tuning. An utterance-level contrastive loss regularizes encoder representations without architectural modification or explicit accent supervision. Experiments on the L2-ARCTIC benchmark show consistent WER reductions across multiple pretrained encoders, with up to 25—29% relative reduction under unseen-accent evaluation. Analysis using within-transcript cosine dispersion indicates that SupCon promotes more compact and stable representation geometry under accent variability. Overall, SupCon provides an effective and model-agnostic regularization strategy for improving accent robustness.

items.title: Exploring the potential and limitations of Model Merging for Multi-Domain Adaptation in ASR
items.abstract: Model merging is a scalable alternative to multi-task training that combines the capabilities of multiple specialised models into a single model. This is particularly attractive for large speech foundation models, which are typically adapted through domain-specific fine-tuning, resulting in multiple customised checkpoints, for which repeating full fine-tuning when new data becomes available is computationally prohibitive. In this work, we study model merging for multi-domain ASR and benchmark 11 merging algorithms for 10 European Portuguese domains, evaluating in-domain accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, as well as English and multilingual performance. We further propose BoostedTSV-M, a new merging algorithm based on TSV-M that mitigates rank collapse via singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability. Overall, our approach outperforms full fine-tuning on European Portuguese while preserving out-of-distribution generalisation in a single model.

items.title: Activation Steering for Accent Adaptation in Large Audio Language Models
items.abstract: Accent variability remains a major source of errors in automatic speech recognition, yet most adaptation methods rely on parameter fine-tuning without understanding where accent information is encoded. We treat accent variation as an interpretable subspace in hidden representations and investigate whether it can be identified and controlled directly in activation space. We extract layer-wise encoder activations and estimate mean-shift directions capturing accent-induced representation shifts. By injecting these directions into individual layers and measuring how they align accented and standard embeddings, we derive a layer-wise accent sensitivity profile, revealing that accent information concentrates in a narrow band of middle encoder layers. Leveraging this structure, we further introduce parameter-free accent steering that modifies representations during inference without updating model weights. Experiments across eight accents show consistent word error rate reductions.

items.title: AccentDrift: Real-time Streaming Accent Conversion via Sparse Speech Tokenization
items.abstract: Although recent speech AI advances have enabled real-time speech understanding and generation, real-time accent conversion (AC) for second-language (L2) speakers in real-world interactions remains underexplored. In this paper, we present AccentDrift, a real-time streaming AC system that preserves linguistic content and speaker identity while transforming speech into a target accent with low latency. From an information bottleneck perspective, we adopt sparse speech tokenization to extract linguistic information from continuous speech. An accent adapter injects accent style into sparse semantic tokens, followed by a timbre adapter that hierarchically generates speaker-specific acoustics. To support streaming, we adopt a cache-aware streaming architecture and parallel streams, achieving 520 ms latency. AccentDrift outperforms prior parallel AC models, and demonstrates the feasibility of generating native-like accents for L2 speakers. Audio samples are available at https://accentdrift.github.io/demo/.

items.title: Mitigating Speaker Leakage in Cascaded Multi-talker ASR with Diarization-based Transcript Correction
items.abstract: While cascaded multi-talker ASR (MT-ASR) leverages state-of-the-art foundation models, its performance is often capped by speaker leakage during separation. Prior correction strategies primarily focus on lexical re-labeling for speaker attribution. We propose a complementary pruning-based paradigm that robustly identifies and removes leakage artifacts. Our method utilizes a pre-trained speaker diarization model as a multimodal verifier to prune transcribed segments satisfying a tripartite consensus of temporal containment, lexical cross-validation, and temporal alignment. Results on LibriMix, LibriSpeechMix, and the AMI Meeting corpus show our algorithm consistently reduces cpWER across diverse overlap conditions. Specifically, on subsets with high speaker leakage, our method achieves relative cpWER reductions of up to 29%, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing the reliability of cascaded MT-ASR transcripts in complex acoustic environments.

items.title: Beyond Mimicry: Constrained Exploration with GRPO for Joint Multi-Talker ASR and Diarization under Unknown Speaker Counts
items.abstract: Joint multi-talker ASR with speaker attribution and timestamps is particularly challenging when the speaker count is unknown and the output must follow a strict structure. We observe that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-only alignment of Speech-LLMs is brittle under dense overlaps, often leading to burst hallucinations and malformed speaker/timestamp tags. We propose a unified two-stage generative framework: (i) CoT-augmented SFT that infers the global speaker count before transcription, and (ii) GRPO-based constrained exploration guided by a Multi-dimensional Constraint-Aware Reward (MCAR) that directly optimizes permutation-invariant accuracy while enforcing counting, temporal, and structural constraints. On Libri3Mix and a Dynamic-Mix (2+3) set (speaker count unknown at test time), our model achieves 14.52%/9.24% cpWER and 1.95%/1.12% WDER, respectively, with GRPO yielding a 35%/54% relative cpWER reduction over SFT+CoT.

items.title: KFC-KWS: Keyframe Fusion with CTC for User-Defined Keyword Spotting
items.abstract: User-defined keyword spotting (KWS) enables personalized voice interaction by detecting user-specified keywords. A key challenge in this task is distinguishing target keywords from phonetically confusable alternatives. To address this challenge, we propose KFC-KWS, a multimodal framework that leverages connectionist temporal classification (CTC)-guided keyframe selection. Specifically, we exploit the peaky posterior distributions of CTC to identify high-confidence phoneme frames, enabling precise alignment across audio, phoneme, and text modalities. These keyframes are then fused with full-utterance representations through cross-attention to capture both local discriminative cues and global contextual information. On LibriPhrase, KFC-KWS achieves the best-balanced performance (98.73% AUC) and substantially outperforms advanced baselines on the challenging hard subset (97.65% AUC and 7.75% EER), demonstrating its effectiveness in discriminating between highly confusable keywords.

items.title: Avoiding Catastrophic Forgetting in Text-Only Adaptation of LLM-based ASR via Multi-View Text Denoising
items.abstract: Adapting LLM-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to new domains using text-only data is challenging. Naively fine-tuning the LLM on target text disrupts the speech-text alignment learned by the projector, causing catastrophic forgetting. We propose a lightweight text-only adaptation strategy that formulates adaptation as a denoising task and introduces a multi-view noise-driven batching scheme to preserve alignment. Each mini-batch mixes paired source audio-text examples, projector-induced noisy transcripts, synthetically corrupted source transcripts, and corrupted target transcripts. This mixing enables domain adaptation while maintaining speech-text alignment. Our method requires no architectural changes or additional parameters and achieves up to 25.4% relative WER improvement over the non-adapted base model, outperforming recent text-only adaptation methods.

items.title: AQA-TTRL: Self-Adaptation in Audio Question Answering with Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) exhibit strong capabilities in general audio understanding but remain static after deployment, limiting their adaptability to real-world data. Since supervised fine-tuning is costly, we propose AQA-TTRL, a novel framework for audio understanding that enables on-the-fly evolution via test-time reinforcement learning using only unlabeled test data. It generates pseudo-labels via majority voting and optimizes the model through reinforcement learning. To address the noise in self-generated labels, we introduce confidence weighting to adjust training signals. Furthermore, multiple-attempt sampling mitigates advantage collapse and stabilizes training. Across MMAU, MMAR, and MMSU, AQA-TTRL achieves significant average improvements of 4.42% for Qwen2.5-Omni 7B and 11.04% for the 3B model. Notably, the adapted 3B model outperforms direct inference of the unadapted 7B model, highlighting the effectiveness of test-time adaptation in audio understanding.

items.title: AFG-Bias: Acoustic-Fusion-Gated Biasing for Plug-and-Play Hotword Customization in LLM-Based ASR
items.abstract: LLM-based ASR achieves strong transcription but struggles with rare domain-specific entities. Prior biasing methods either require architecture-specific training or rely on prompt injection, which suffers from scale collapse and hallucination. We propose AFG-Bias, a plug-and-play framework grounding hotword biasing in acoustic evidence without modifying LLM parameters. Cross-Modal Acoustic Retrieval (CAR) selects relevant hotwords from a large candidate list via sliding-window alignment, and Acoustic-Fusion Gating injects verified bias into decoding while suppressing hallucinations. On three LLM-ASR backbones, AFG-Bias achieves up to 74.1% relative CER reduction in financial and medical domains, and improves AISHELL-1 hotword F1 by up to 5.4 absolute points.

items.title: Decoding the Trade-off: A Large-Scale Analysis of Latency and Stability in LLM-based Speech Translation Cascades
items.abstract: Real-time subtitling must balance low latency with stable translations. In segment-level cloud cascades, aggressive endpointing increases request rate and can push utilization beyond service capacity, triggering a backlog avalanche in which queueing delay dominates and "fast" settings become slower in steady state. We present RST, a reproducible KO→EN subtitle pipeline that distinguishes time-to-first-text (latency_first) and time-to-stable-text (latency_stable). On the full FLEURS corpus, we show that aggressive endpointing drives cascades into a backlog regime (median RTF > 1), where latency_stable grows over time. Whisper prompt conditioning further degrades short-chunk streaming ASR by +14-17 pp CER and can leak instructions. Sweeps reveal a clear stability boundary. We define an operational threshold as the most aggressive setting with median RTF ≤1, showing that throughput stability is essential for low-latency LLM-based cascades.

items.title: Fed-SpeechLLM: Federated Learning Speech Language Models for Multilingual ASR
items.abstract: SpeechLLMs show strong promise for multilingual ASR, yet centralized training conflicts with privacy constraints over distributed, linguistically diverse data. This paper presents Fed-SpeechLLM, a federated learning framework for multilingual SpeechLLM-based ASR evaluated on a bilingual English and Italian setting. We study federated optimization under compounded non-IID conditions from acoustic and cross-lingual heterogeneity. Standard FL methods degrade when clients hold language-skewed distributions. Moreover, we propose language-aware gradient aggregation and a sampling clustering-based method to mitigate multilingual imbalance, using selective aggregation of speech encoders and projection layers with a frozen LLM backbone. Results confirm competitive performance against centralized training.

items.title: Multi-Channel Differential ASR for Robust Wearer Speech Recognition on Smart Glasses
items.abstract: With the growing adoption of wearable devices such as smart glasses for AI assistants, wearer speech recognition (WSR) is becoming increasingly critical to next-generation human-computer interfaces. However, in real environments, interference from side-talk speech remains a significant challenge to WSR and may cause accumulated errors for downstream tasks such as natural language processing. In this work, we introduce a novel multi-channel differential automatic speech recognition (ASR) method for robust WSR on smart glasses. The proposed system takes differential inputs from different frontends that complement each other to improve the robustness of WSR, including a beamformer, microphone selection, and a lightweight side-talk detection model. Evaluations on both simulated and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms the traditional approach, achieving up to an 18.0% relative reduction in word error rate.

items.title: ESPnet3: Infrastructure for Scalable Speech and Audio Research in the Foundation Model Era
items.abstract: Recent speech research involves increasingly large datasets, complex models, and diverse experimental workflows. However, existing frameworks require substantial engineering effort to support such experiments. We present ESPnet3, a speech and audio research framework built on a modular system architecture with configuration-driven dataset composition and unified Python-based workflows. ESPnet3 introduces a DataOrganizer abstraction for flexible dataset integration and dataset sharding for memory-efficient large-scale training, while allowing recipe-specific logic through lightweight stage overrides. In OWSM pre-training experiments, ESPnet3 reduces per-epoch training time by 21.1 minutes compared to ESPnet2 and achieves >80% GPU utilization in multi-node training. Fine-tuning experiments show that new models and datasets can be integrated with around 46 lines of additional code. ESPnet3 will be publicly released with model checkpoints and training logs.

items.title: SCRIBE: Diagnostic Evaluation and Rich Transcription Models for Indic ASR
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition replaces typing only when correction costs less than manual entry, a threshold determined by error types, not counts: fixing a misrecognized domain term costs far more than inserting a comma. Word error rate (WER) fails on two fronts: it collapses distinct error categories into a single scalar, and it structurally penalizes agglutinative languages where valid sandhi merges inflate scores. We introduce SCRIBE, a diagnostic framework that provides categorical error decomposition into lexical, punctuation, numeral, and domain-entity rates through sandhi-tolerant alignment with domain vocabulary injection. Human validation confirms SCRIBE aligns with expert judgment where WER does not. We release SCRIBE, an LLM curation pipeline, benchmarks, and open-weight rich transcription models for Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada.

items.title: Audio-KWS-Gated Error Memory Retrieval for Incremental ASR Post-Correction
items.abstract: ASR has improved, yet rare and domain-specific terms remain challenging. LLMs enable second-pass post-correction without retraining an ASR model. In long-running use, correction logs can be reused to fix recurring errors, but full-history prompting is limited by the LLM context window, and text-only selection is brittle when trigger terms are misrecognized. We propose an incremental post-correction framework with Audio-KWS-gated retrieval, where Audio-KWS detects keywords from audio to select relevant correction records within the context window. We proceed in three steps: (i) LLM-based error analysis extracts correction pairs to update a keyword inventory, (ii) Audio-KWS runs on audio to detect Top-N keywords and retrieve correction records (using phonetic readings as keywords for Japanese), and (iii) the LLM applies record-guided edits. On Earnings-21 and CSJ, our method achieves about 70% prompt reduction (Top-20 English; Top-10 Japanese) while improving WER/CER and Bias-F1.

items.title: Rubric-Aligned Disentangled Evaluation of Human Simultaneous Interpreting
items.abstract: Human simultaneous interpreting (SI) is commonly assessed with analytic rubrics separating meaning transfer, delivery quality, and temporal synchrony, yet no automatic metric is designed for rubric-aligned segment-level SI evaluation. We construct a professionally annotated corpus of 1,101 SI segments with scores for meaning transfer (LQ), delivery quality (EXP), and perceived latency (LAT). We show that structured LLM prompting and scalar supervision collapse rubric dimensions, yielding near-zero correlation with human ratings and strong cross-dimension coupling. To isolate supervision structure under identical backbone capacity, we introduce dual regression heads on a LoRA-adapted COMET-KIWI encoder. On a held-out talk-level test set, the model achieves Pearson correlations of 0.388 (LQ) and 0.301 (EXP), improving over frozen COMET-KIWI. Given low absolute rater agreement, we interpret results relative to human consistency and target stable ranking signals for formative assessment.

items.title: ARTIST: Universal Articulatory Space Modeling for Multilingual Indic-to-English Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.abstract: We present ARTIST, a novel end-to-end framework for multilingual Indic-to-English Speech-to-Speech Translation (S2ST) operating in a universal articulatory space. It utilizes a Conformer encoder with intermediate CTC supervision over source articulatory features, explicitly aligning diverse acoustic inputs with quantized, language-agnostic representations. To map these features, we introduce a Convolution-Augmented Differential Transformer decoder designed to capture both local phonetic nuances and global context. We demonstrate exceptional cross-lingual transfer across 11 Indic languages, including extreme low-resource settings (10hr/language). For instance, with only 166M parameters, ARTIST outperforms the 1.2B parameter SeamlessM4T baseline on BLEU, COMET, and chrF. ARTIST also achieves superior VRAM efficiency, establishing a high-performance paradigm for scaling direct S2ST to resource-constrained environments.

items.title: Evaluating and Preserving Lexical Stress in English-to-Chinese Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) systems have achieved impressive progress in semantic accuracy and speech naturalness. However, the cross-lingual transfer of lexical stress-a vital cue for emphasis and speaker intent-remains heavily under-explored, compounded by a lack of reliable automatic evaluation metrics for tonal languages like Chinese. We investigate English-to-Chinese S2ST stress transfer by constructing a stress-annotated Chinese dataset and an XLS-R-based Mandarin stress detector. Integrating this with the English EmphAssess system, we propose a novel objective metric for cross-lingual stress evaluation. Furthermore, we fine-tune CosyVoice3 to build a stress-aware S2ST system. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed S2ST architecture significantly outperforms existing systems in stress translation capability while maintaining competitive translation quality. Furthermore, our evaluation metric exhibits a strong correlation with human subjective judgments.

items.title: Listening or Reading? Evaluating Speech Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Speech-to-Text Translation
items.abstract: Speech-to-Text Translation (S2TT) systems that cascade Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Text Translation (T2TT) are fundamentally limited by error propagation and the loss of prosodic cues. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting was introduced to address these limitations by providing joint access to both speech and transcription during generation. In this study, we systematically evaluate CoT's actual speech awareness through input attribution analysis, assessment of robustness against corrupted transcripts, and prosody-awareness evaluation. Our results indicate that CoT largely replicates cascaded behavior, relying heavily on textual transcripts. By applying simple training interventions (e.g., injecting noisy transcripts in the CoT), we demonstrate enhanced model robustness and increased acoustic reliance. Our findings challenge the presumed benefits of CoT S2TT and emphasize the necessity for techniques that help integrate acoustic information into the translation process.

items.title: A Multimodal Semi-Supervised Framework for Automatic Construction of a Cross-Lingual Taigi Speech-Chinese Subtitle Corpus
items.abstract: The lack of labeled data for low-resource languages such as Taigi (Taiwanese) limits AI development. This work addresses the issue by exploiting online videos containing Taigi speech with hard-coded Chinese subtitles. We propose a multimodal semi-supervised framework that combines a trimodal Audio-Visual-Language Model (AVLM) with an iterative pseudo-labeling process inspired by knowledge distillation. A Vision-Language Model fuses OCR outputs and AVLM predictions to generate refined subtitles, enabling automatic construction of a large-scale Taigi speech-Chinese subtitle corpus from unlabeled videos. Experiments show that the AVLM reduces subtitle recognition CER from 36.8% to 9.3%. The resulting 860-hour corpus improves downstream tasks: Whisper's cross-lingual transcription CER decreases from 57.8% to 37.8%, and Taigi-Chinese translation BLEU doubles from 0.2016 to 0.4033. These results demonstrate an effective and transferable paradigm for low-resource corpus construction.

items.title: AfriVox-v2: A Domain-Verticalized Benchmark for In-the-Wild African Speech Recognition
items.abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) show strong speech recognition and translation capabilities for high-resource languages. However, African languages remain dramatically underrepresented in benchmarks, limiting their practical use in low-resource settings. While early benchmarks tested African languages and accents, they lacked exhaustive real-world noise and granular domain evaluations. We present AfriVox-v2, a comprehensive benchmark designed to test speech models under realistic African deployment conditions. AfriVox-v2 introduces "in the wild" unscripted audio for all supported languages. We also introduce strict domain verticalization, evaluating model accuracy across ten sectors including government, finance, health, and agriculture and conducting targeted tests on numbers and named entities. Finally, we benchmark a new generation of speech models, including Sahara-v2, Gemini 3 Flash, and the Omnilingual CTC models. Our results expose the true generalization gap of modern speech models in specialized, noisy African contexts and provide a reliable blueprint for developers building localized voice AI.

items.title: From Dispersion to Attraction: Spectral Dynamics of Hallucination Across Whisper Model Scales
items.abstract: Hallucinations in large ASR models present a critical safety risk. In this work, we propose the Spectral Sensitivity Theorem, which predicts a phase transition in deep networks from a dispersive regime (signal decay) to an attractor regime (rank-1 collapse) governed by layer-wise gain and alignment. We validate this theory by analyzing the eigenspectra of activation graphs in Whisper models (Tiny to Large-v3-Turbo) under adversarial stress. Our results are consistent with the theoretical prediction: intermediate models exhibit Structural Disintegration (Regime I), characterized by a 13.4% collapse in Cross-Attention rank. Conversely, large models enter a Compression-Seeking Attractor state (Regime II), where Self-Attention actively compresses rank (-2.34%) and hardens the spectral slope, decoupling the model from acoustic evidence.

items.title: Error Diversity and Performance Variability in Zero-Shot Children's Speech Recognition
items.abstract: Children's speech recognition remains challenging due to acoustic variability and limited labeled data. This study analyzes the behavior of self-supervised learning (SSL) representations for children's speech recognition under a strict zero-shot adult-to-child transfer setting. Layer-wise representations from Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, and Data2Vec are evaluated using hybrid ASR systems trained only on adult speech. Although several layers achieve comparable best-case word error rates, substantial variability exists across representations. Error analysis reveals dataset-dependent error structures, while LLM-based post-recognition correction provides little improvement. Oracle analysis further shows that different layers capture complementary acoustic information, particularly under stronger domain mismatch. These findings indicate that recognition errors are primarily driven by acoustic representation limitations rather than recoverable linguistic inconsistencies.

items.title: Gender Bias in ASR: A Controlled Study of Gender Composition Across Training Paradigms
items.abstract: Gender disparities in ASR are commonly attributed to training data imbalance, often evaluated by fine-tuning pretrained systems on gender-controlled splits. We test whether such fine-tuning reveals a systematic relationship between training composition and gender disparity. Across three pretrained models and 11 splits spanning 0-100% female representation, male and female WERs fluctuate without consistent direction, yielding no systematic composition-disparity relationship. To determine whether the effect exists, we include a from-scratch system as a controlled reference under identical conditions. In contrast, this system exhibits consistent, directional disparity shifts as composition varies, confirming that the effect is real but masked in pretrained models by representations established during large-scale pretraining. These results demonstrate that balancing fine-tuning data alone is insufficient to mitigate gender disparity in pretrained ASR.

items.title: Balancing ASR and diarization in end-to-end LLMs for multi-talker speech recognition
items.abstract: Multi-talker speech recognition is often addressed by combining automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker diarization in a pipeline system. Recently, LLM-based approaches have shown promise by jointly modeling semantic and speaker information, but they typically require large-scale multi-talker corpora that are costly to annotate. In this paper, we investigate how to efficiently train an LLM-based system with limited real-recorded data while maintaining high accuracy in speaker attribution. We propose several strategies: (1) a dual-encoder architecture to extract semantic and speaker features, (2) a feature interleaving format to merge these features as the inputs to the LLM, (3) a length-aware speaker ID loss to enhance diarization capability, and (4) an adaptive threshold strategy for ASR loss computation to mitigate hallucinations caused by speech overlaps. These strategies balance training between ASR and diarization tasks. Our system outperforms open-source baseline approaches, achieving relative improvements of 18% on the Al-iMeeting corpus and 24% on the Aishell4 corpus.

items.title: Multi-Talker ASR Unaffected by Speaker Change Count
items.abstract: We develop an autoregressive model for multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) robust to the number of speaker changes. Recent studies on multi-talker ASR handle multiple speakers by recursively estimating a single token sequence formed by concatenating their transcripts with speaker change tokens. However, as this technique heavily relies on context including speaker change tokens, inference performance degrades when the number of speaker changes exceeds those in the training data. To address this limitation, we estimate the token sequence, including speaker change tokens, without relying on how many speaker changes have occurred. This is achieved by introducing a novel speaker change token mask in self-attention, which sets the values of speaker change tokens and randomly selected tokens referenced by other queries to zero, preventing the model from inferring the number of speaker changes from context. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

items.title: WildElder: A Chinese Elderly Speech Dataset from the Wild with Fine-Grained Manual Annotations
items.abstract: Elderly speech poses unique challenges for automatic processing due to age-related changes such as slower articulation and vocal tremors. Existing Chinese datasets are mostly recorded in controlled environments, limiting their diversity and real-world applicability. To address this gap, we present WildElder, a Mandarin elderly speech corpus collected from online videos and enriched with fine-grained manual annotations, including transcription, speaker age, gender, and accent strength. Combining the realism of in-the-wild data with expert curation, WildElder enables robust research on automatic speech recognition and speaker profiling. Experimental results reveal both the difficulties of elderly speech recognition and the potential of WildElder as a challenging new benchmark. The dataset and code have been available at https://github.com/NKU-HLT/WildElder.

items.title: Post-ASR Proper Noun Grounding via Multi-View Phonetic and Semantic Retrieval
items.abstract: Modern end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems achieve strong overall transcription accuracy but remain vulnerable to proper nouns and long-tail vocabulary. Such errors are often phonetically plausible yet lexically incorrect, degrading downstream systems that rely on accurate entity interpretation. We propose a post-ASR proper noun grounding framework that links noisy mentions to ranked candidates from a predefined lexicon without retraining or modifying the ASR model. The method integrates complementary similarity views: fine-grained phonetic representations via grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P), coarse phonetic encoding using Soundex, and context-aware semantic embeddings, with normalized score fusion for unified ranking. Multi-view fusion increases Recall@1 over vanilla exact match by 36.4 and 23.6 percentage points for Whisper-large-v3 and Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, reaching 74.67% and 59.82% respectively, with up to 87.36% Recall@10 in the strongest configuration.

items.title: From Text Metrics to Model Internals: A Study of Whisper ASR Hallucination Detection
items.abstract: Hallucinations of ASR models — fluent transcriptions with no basis in audio — degrade system performance and pose risks in downstream applications. Robust detection of such errors remains a challenge. This paper studies Whisper large v3 hallucination detection on real-speech human-annotated data across three paradigms: text-based, LLM-based, and internal decoder state probing. Text classifiers utilizing metrics for text evaluation achieve high recall but degrade without reference transcripts. LLM-based detection improves precision with domain-specific prompt conditioning, yet remains less competitive than the lightweight text-based methods. Probing Whisper's decoder representations, without a ground-truth reference, yields the strongest performance, revealing that hallucination traits are encoded across intermediate decoding layers. A late-fusion meta-classifier combining text and internal-state outputs achieves the best overall detection performance.

items.title: Grounding Whisper: An Audio Anchor-Based Approach for Hallucination Mitigation and Throughput-Efficient ASR
items.abstract: Whisper exhibits robust ASR performance but suffers from hallucinations on silence and non-speech audio, generating spurious transcriptions that undermine production reliability. We introduce anchor audio, a simple input-level technique that prepends a short audio phrase with near-zero domain occurrence to the input, enabling hallucination detection without modifying or fine-tuning the model. Using this mechanism, we evaluate five inference approaches ranging from single-call augmentation to batch concatenation with automatic fallback, exploring accuracy-latency-throughput trade-offs. Our batch strategy leverages Whisper's fixed 30-second window to concatenate multiple short utterances while maintaining fidelity through anchor-based validation. This reduces overall WER from 32.18% to 13.23%, achieves 0.14% Hallucination Error Rate on non-speech audio, and preserves latency comparable to baseline VAD pipelines, demonstrating an effective, practical solution for hallucination mitigation.

title: New Architecture and Analyses for ASR and Speech LMs

items.title: Convolutional Dynamic Rotary Positional Encoding
items.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is a strong alternative to relative positional encoding in modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) encoder models. However, its discrete, uniformly-spaced chronological index is misaligned with the continuous, semantic nature of speech features. We propose Convolutional Dynamic RoPE (CD-RoPE), a dynamic positional encoding complementing Branchformer's attention path by warping the rotary temporal index conditioned on local acoustic context via a lightweight depthwise-separable convolution. Additive position modulation preserves RoPE's harmonic structure, enabling continuous input-dependent shifts. CD-RoPE achieves consistent WER improvements over RelPos on Branchformer across all LibriSpeech test sets with 2.2M fewer parameters. Targeted robustness evaluation on Speech Robust Bench (SRB) confirms that CD-RoPE's advantage is strongest under temporal perturbations, validating the temporal warping mechanism.

items.title: Diffusion Language Models for Speech Recognition
items.abstract: Diffusion language models have recently emerged as a leading alternative to standard language models, due to their ability for bidirectional attention and parallel text generation. In this work, we explore variants for their use in speech recognition. Specifically, we introduce a comprehensive guide to incorporating masked diffusion language models (MDLM) and uniform-state diffusion models (USDMs) for rescoring ASR hypotheses. Additionally, we designed a new joint-decoding method that combines CTC and USDM by integrating the framewise probability distributions derived from CTC with the labelwise probability distributions computed by USDM at each decoding step, thereby generating new candidates that combine strong language knowledge from USDM and acoustic information from CTC. Our findings reveal that USDM, as well as MDLM, can significantly improve the accuracy of recognised text. We publish all our code and recipes.

items.title: Do speech foundation models really learn words?
items.abstract: Self-supervised speech foundation models are now used in a wide array of downstream applications, including traditional speech recognition and as the basis for tokens in speech-aware language models. Attempts to understand their usefulness have largely focused on probing their representations' ability to discriminate phonemes and words. However, discriminative ability for words need not imply specialized representation of words per se. Good discrimination of words may be explained by good encoding of word form (phonemes) rather than form-independent word representations encoding identity or syntactic/semantic properties. By partialling out phoneme information using residualization, we show that, in later layers, HuBERT and wav2vec 2.0 do in general learn representations which encode words with reasonable fidelity independently of local phonetic content. We show that this simple approach to disentanglement can enhance higher-order linguistic information in word discovery tasks.

items.title: Readability Does Not Predict Speech Recognition Errors: Contrasting Human and Machine Perception.
items.abstract: This study challenges the historical link between the readability of a text and its intelligibility by automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. While textual complexity has a significant impact on human comprehension, its effect on modern end-to-end architectures remains unclear. We present a controlled experimental pipeline using the CLEAR corpus, speech synthesis, and acoustic degradations (babble noise, reverberation). Our results demonstrate a near-perfect decoupling between readability, measured by the Global Readability Index, and intelligibility, measured by the Word Error Rate. This orthogonality persists under different acoustic degradations and is validated on natural speech. The absence of a "cognitive load" on the model during the transcription process confirms that it is now completely independent of textual complexity.

items.title: Probing Linguistic Information in Speech Embeddings: A Diagnostic Analysis across Acoustic and Structural Domains
items.abstract: Speech embeddings have become a central component of modern automatic speech recognition and speech-language models; however, their linguistic interpretability is still under active research. This study adopts a diagnostic approach to examine the extent to which speech embeddings encode linguistic features. We analyse linear associations between pretrained acoustic embeddings and a set of core acoustic, phonetic, and linguistic structure features. The results show that embeddings encode acoustic and phonetic properties, particularly temporal dynamics, spectral structure, and voice-quality related features, while higher-level linguistic structure is represented more weakly. Lexical complexity shows a measurable association, whereas morphological and syntactic complexity show limited linear accessibility. These findings suggest that embeddings capture linguistic information in a distributed and gradient manner, with strongest sensitivity to properties closely tied to signal realisation.

items.title: I Am No One: Style-Aware Paraphrasing for Text Anonymization
items.abstract: Authorship attribution models can re-identify users from seemingly anonymized text by exploiting stable stylistic fingerprints, even after explicit identifiers are removed, posing a growing privacy risk for text publishing and analytics. This risk extends to speech-derived text such as ASR transcripts of meetings and call-center conversations, where stylometric leakage can persist even after acoustic anonymization. Differential privacy-based anonymization often severely degrades text quality and utility. We propose a style-aware, prompt-driven anonymization approach that uses pretrained large language models to construct compact stylistic profiles from minimal samples and rewrite text to suppress identifiable style markers while preserving meaning. Across blog and review datasets, our approach reduces authorship attribution F1 by 60-70% while maintaining content quality and readability, substantially outperforming DP-based and non-DP baselines.

items.title: Reducing the Offline-Streaming Gap for Unified ASR Transducer with Consistency Regularization
items.abstract: Unification of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems reduces development and maintenance costs, but training a single model to perform well in both offline and low-latency streaming settings remains challenging. We present a Unified ASR framework for Transducer (RNNT) training that supports both offline and streaming decoding within a single model, using chunk-limited attention with right context and dynamic chunked convolutions. To further close the gap between offline and streaming performance, we introduce an efficient Triton implementation of mode-consistency regularization for RNNT (MCR-RNNT), which encourages agreement across training modes. Experiments show that the proposed approach improves streaming accuracy at low latency while preserving offline performance and scaling to larger model sizes and training datasets. The proposed Unified ASR framework and the English model checkpoint are open-sourced.

items.title: BACON: Boundary-Aware Convolution for Streaming Conformer Models
items.abstract: We propose Boundary-Aware CONvolution (BACON), a drop-in replacement for causal convolution in streaming sequence tasks that leverage chunk-based Conformers. Streaming Conformers typically pair chunked attention with causal convolution to prevent future information leakage. We show that causal convolution is unnecessarily restrictive: within a chunk, all frames are already available, so the convolution kernel can safely look ahead up to the chunk boundary without violating the streaming constraint. BACON exploits this by splitting the depthwise convolution channels into a causal group and a boundary-aware bidirectional group, yielding a wider effective receptive field than the causal baseline while preserving parameter count. Across single-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), multi-speaker ASR, and speech-to-text translation tasks with two model architectures, BACON improves model accuracy while maintaining comparable latency.

items.title: Progressive Alignment Objectives for Aligner-Encoder based ASR
items.abstract: Aligner-Encoders are recently proposed seq2seq end-to-end ASR models that replace decoder attention by predicting the u-th token directly from the u-th encoder position, so the encoder must learn the alignment internally without cross-attention or a transducer lattice. In practice, this alignment often forms abruptly in the upper layers, making training sensitive and brittle on long utterances. We propose InterAligner, which adds an intermediate Aligner objective so alignment can form progressively across depth, together with an intermediate CTC loss (InterCTC) to stabilize optimization. On LibriSpeech with a 17-layer Conformer, a final-only Aligner reaches 5.0/7.8 WER (test-clean/other). InterCTC improves to 3.4/6.0, and InterAligner further reduces WER to 3.1/5.6 with the largest gains on long utterances.

items.title: From Bilevel to Trilevel: Joint Training for Speech Recognition
items.abstract: This paper presents the practical optimization strategies to extend the bilevel learning into a trilevel setting for speech recognition. This method jointly trains an acoustic model according to supervised, unsupervised, and distilled learning objectives. To make trilevel training feasible in large-scale ASR models, we employ a sequential penalty-based bilevel gradient descent method that collapses the lower two levels into a bilevel subproblem and then integrates it with the upper level. This formulation allows the model to leverage the general structure from unlabeled data, the task-specific alignment from labeled speech, and the knowledge transfer from a teacher network within a single optimization loop. The experiments on LibriSpeech with a FastConformer backbone demonstrate that these strategies yield the consistent improvements over the conventional two-stage pre-training and fine-tuning pipeline, as well as over the prior bilevel optimization methods.

items.title: LLM-as-Joiner: Decoupling Alignment from Language Modeling in Label-synchronous ASR
items.abstract: We present LLM-as-Joiner, an LLM-based ASR architecture that decouples speech-text alignment from language modeling. A speech encoder first converts an input of T acoustic frames into U token-level speech states, one per output token, following the Aligner-Encoder framework. A pretrained LLM then predicts the transcript from these U states, with speech injected at a chosen LLM layer; only upper LLM layers are adapted via LoRA. Compared to conventional decoder-only speech-as-prefix decoding, the LLM operates on a shorter context (U rather than T + U), reducing memory and compute. On LibriSpeech and multilingual Common Voice, the proposed LLM-as-Joiner outperforms size-matched baselines, and joint training with a lightweight recognizer yields additional gains in the lightweight head, suggesting implicit transfer of linguistic knowledge from the LLM to the speech encoder.

items.title: Accurate Source-Free Speech Classification via Meta-Learned Target-Centric Model Merging
items.abstract: How can we build a speech classifier for an unseen domain when access to source-domain data is unavailable? Speech classification is widely used (e.g., voice commands, emotion recognition, etc.), but it is highly sensitive to domain shifts (e.g., languages), often causing substantial performance degradation. This issue becomes critical when source data cannot be accessed and only pretrained source models with limited target data are available. Under such constraints, typical adaptation approaches are inapplicable, and existing model merging methods easily overfit the limited target data. We propose Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ, an accurate target-centric model merging framework that combines multiple pretrained source models using limited target data. To improve generalization under scarce target labels, Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ exploits meta-learning to resolve representation misalignment and emphasize target-relevant sources. Extensive experiments show that Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ outperforms the baselines by up to 14.5 points in Macro-F1.

items.title: LLM-HB: Language-Aware LLM-Guided Hotword Biasing for Code-Switching ASR
items.abstract: Code-switching (CS) speech, characterized by language alternation within a single utterance, is prevalent in multilingual communities and poses challenges to automatic speech recognition (ASR) due to rapid language transitions. We propose LLM-HB, a language-aware large language model-guided hotword biasing framework for code-switching ASR (CS-ASR). The framework incorporates a mixture-of-experts (MoE) adaptor and an auxiliary language prediction head to better capture and differentiate multilingual representations, while hotwords are injected through LLM-based prompting. Experiments on the ASRU2019 code-switching challenge test set demonstrate that LLM-HB achieves a 20.30% relative reduction in mixed error rate (MER) over the baseline, reaching 5.85% MER under a 15-distractor hotword setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate LLM-guided biasing into code-switching ASR. We further release the extracted ASRU2019 hotword list to support future research.

items.title: Improving Code-Switching ASR with Code-Mixing Guided Synthetic Speech
items.abstract: Code-switch (CS) Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) remains challenging due to limited availability of high quality CS text-speech pairs for training. Although synthetic data augmentation via text-to-speech (TTS) has been explored, existing CS TTS approaches primarily optimise reconstruction fidelity and do not explicitly enforce language-boundary consistency, thereby limiting their effectiveness for CS ASR augmentation. This paper proposes a code-mixing guided preference-learning framework that steers synthetic speech generation toward improved code-switching fidelity using the Code Mixing Index (CMI). Experiments on the SEAME Mandarin-English conversational corpus demonstrate that the proposed method enhances the utility of synthetic data for ASR fine-tuning. Specifically, when fine-tuning Whisper Large, the proposed approach reduces Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 12.1%/17.8% to 8.9%/14.2% on the DevMAN and DevSGE sets, respectively.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning for Data-Efficient Code-Switched ASR
items.abstract: Audio-language models can be prompted for code-switched speech, but their decoding is not optimized for code-switching and often fails at language boundaries. We propose a practical reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards recipe for data-efficient adaptation of audio-language models to code-switched ASR using group relative policy optimization, combining an error rate reward with a script fidelity reward that penalizes wrong writing systems and a two-pass draft-and-refinement procedure. Using Qwen2-Audio as a reproducible testbed across 10 language pairs, training on only TTS code-switched speech, we show that RLVR with 10% of the data matches LoRA supervised fine-tuning trained on the full dataset, with the largest gains on typologically distant pairs. The error rate reward eliminates translation errors while the script fidelity reward separately reduces script contamination without degradation. These gains transfer zero-shot to a human-recorded code-switching corpus.

items.title: Direct Preference Optimization for English-Mandarin Code-Switching Speech Recognition in Audio LLMs
items.abstract: Audio large language models (Audio LLMs) exhibit systematic failures in transcribing code-switching speech despite strong multilingual capabilities. Focusing on English-Mandarin, we identify three failure modes: language omission, translation-instead-of-transcription, and hallucination. We apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align models, constructing preference pairs in which chosen responses preserve mixed-language content while rejected responses mimic failure patterns. Training three Audio LLMs on 100K pairs (570 hours), we observe consistent behavioral shifts: models learn to preserve language composition rather than translating when prompted for transcription. This alignment yields MER reductions up to 89.6% (in-distribution) and 20.0% (out-of-distribution). Our findings suggest DPO can effectively elicit correct code-switching transcription behavior from multilingual Audio LLMs.

items.title: Adding Robust Code-Switching Capabilities to High Performance Multilingual ASR
items.abstract: Code-switching (CSW) remains challenging for large multilingual ASR systems in real-world deployment. While fine-tuning on synthetic CSW data is possible, it generally degrades strong monolingual baselines. Our goal is to preserve these capabilities while extending models to handle complex code-switching, including morphological variations across languages. We propose Bayesian factorized adaptation, which learns to efficiently integrate switching-relevant knowledge into strong pretrained models without overwriting existing capabilities. Requiring only a small amount of synthetic data, our approach reduces transcription errors by 32.87% on code-switched words while improving overall WER by 5.31%, all while maintaining monolingual performance. Our results demonstrate that effective CSW adaptation depends more on knowledge integration than data complexity.

items.title: Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation
items.abstract: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.

title: Information Extraction and Retrieval / Survey Talk

items.title: Expressive Speech Translation
items.abstract: Speech to speech translation is still a challenging problem, without much consensus about model architectures, training data, evaluation methods, and so on. One frontier in this area is the preservation of the expressiveness of the input speech in the translation. Expressiveness ranges from global properties such as the speaker's voice and emotion as well as acoustic conditions, to local properties such as pauses, varying speaking rates, emphasis, and pitch for individual words. This survey will cover various aspects, such as training data, data synthesis methods, speech representation, model architectures, the use of large language models, and evaluation metrics.

items.title: Personalized Keyword Spotting for User-Defined Keywords Leveraging Text-Independent Speaker Verification
items.abstract: User-defined keyword spotting (UD-KWS) enables zero-shot wake-word detection from text, but existing systems learn speaker-invariant representations that cannot reject impostors uttering the correct keyword. We address this dual zero-shot setting—unseen keywords and unseen speakers—with ZP-KWS, a lightweight framework combining a phoneme-supervised audio encoder with a GE2E-pretrained compact speaker encoder (about 0.9M parameters). Multiplicative late fusion at inference grants each branch independent veto power, supporting modes from conventional detection to strict speaker-gated activation without retraining. On LibriPhrase, Google Speech Commands, and Qualcomm datasets, ZP-KWS reduces target-only FRR at 1% FAR by up to 60% relative to the strongest baseline while maintaining competitive keyword detection, all within a 1.55M parameter budget for edge deployment.

items.title: wav2tok 2.0: Scalable Audio Tokenization Maintaining Explicit Pairwise Token Alignment for Efficient Audio Retrieval
items.abstract: Learning discrete speech representations that preserve similarity across variable-length utterances is central to query-by-example spoken term detection (QbE-STD). While wav2tok introduced CTC-based sequence alignment to enforce token consistency, its tightly coupled clustering and alignment training recipe limits scalability. We propose wav2tok 2.0, a scalable alignment-aware speech tokenizer built on the BEST-STD backbone. wav2tok 2.0 employs staged training, first learning discriminative, speaker-invariant representations via contrastive learning and vector quantization, and then enforcing pairwise token consistency using a CTC alignment loss and a novel DTW-aligned framewise prediction objective with adaptive weighting. Experiments show that wav2tok 2.0 consistently outperforms BEST-STD and general-purpose tokenizers on QbE-STD while remaining efficient and scalable.

items.title: Rethinking Organization Entity Modeling in End-to-End Acoustic Named Entity Recognition
items.abstract: End-to-end acoustic named entity recognition (NER) integrates speech transcription and entity detection within a unified model, avoiding error propagation in cascaded ASR-NER systems. However, organization entities remain significantly harder to detect due to multi-word spans, acronyms, and lexical variability. We present a systematic analysis of organization recognition failures in acoustic NER, revealing that conventional cross-entropy training inadequately models entity span dependencies. To address this limitation, we propose an organization-aware Whisper-based acoustic NER framework combining LLM-based targeted semantic augmentation, category-specific boundary supervision, and a structure-constrained entity learning (SCEL) objective that enforces entity span consistency during decoding. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in organization recognition while maintaining strong ASR performance, outperforming in entity-recognition for several other existing approaches.

items.title: AnySimLite: A Lightweight Few-Shot Similarity Encoder for On-Device Speech-Adjacent Classification
items.abstract: To minimize privacy concerns and inference latency on edge devices like smartphones, lightweight on-device models remain important for end-user applications. Many of these applications involve natural language classification, but deploying multiple specialized models creates a memory footprint challenge. We investigate: Can a single lightweight architecture solve multiple Speech-Adjacent (SA) classification tasks through reduction to a nuanced text similarity formulation? We propose ANYSIM-LITE, a lightweight similarity encoder that combines word-level and character-level channels. Together with a dataset transformation strategy, we evaluate ANYSIM-LITE across multiple SA classification tasks and show that it consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings while maintaining a low memory footprint. Even in the worst case, the performance drop remains below 7% while using < 1/250th of the model size of the SOTA qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.

title: ASR Under Real-World Constraints: Streaming, Adaptation, and Efficiency

items.title: A Compact Fully-Open Cache-Aware Streaming Model for Japanese ASR
items.abstract: We present a 123M-parameter fully-open cache-aware streaming model for Japanese ASR with a hybrid RNNT/CTC design. To our knowledge, no prior Japanese ASR system simultaneously provides full openness—open weights, data preparation details, code, and logs-together with streaming capability. On a 35K-hour pre-training corpus we show that CER-stratified data curation consistently benefits underrepresented domains but can hurt performance under multi-domain fine-tuning with higher decoder capacity. We further study progressive fine-tuning across five domains totaling 507 hours. Evaluated on five test sets, our model achieves 12.4% average CER (RNNT), outperforming the 1B OWSM-CTC v4 (13.5%) and 619M ReazonSpeech NeMo-v2 (14.1%) while being 5-8× smaller, with an RTFx of 1220 (batch) and 446 (streaming).

items.title: Robust Streaming ASR with Decoupled Separation and Recognition
items.abstract: Real-time speech transcription that is robust to background noise, room reverberation, and interfering speakers is critical for many real-world automatic speech recognition (ASR) applications. To address these interferences, multi-condition training (MCT) is commonly employed for training an ASR model, but it requires large-scale training data and degrades recognition performance on clean speech. In this work, we propose a decoupled framework that leverages an online speech separation frontend, and a streaming ASR backend trained only on clean speech, for robust streaming ASR. We benchmark the proposed approach on LibriSpeech, CHiME-4, and LibriCSS datasets, and demonstrate that the decoupled framework consistently outperforms the MCT-based baselines for streaming ASR. Our approach is also shown to generalize to large pre-trained speech models, offering a modular approach for robust streaming ASR that avoids task-specific re-training and MCT.

items.title: Margin-Aware Contrastive Regularization for Robust Streaming Keyword Spotting under Strict False-Alarm Constraints
items.abstract: Edge keyword spotting (KWS) in continuous streaming must satisfy strict false-alarm (FA) budgets while maintaining high detection sensitivity. At stringent points (≤ 0.5 FA/h), CE-trained lightweight causal models suffer severe false rejection rate (FRR) degradation against phonetically similar imposters. We propose Margin-Aware Contrastive Regularization (MACR), an offline auxiliary objective that applies intra-class attraction only to target keywords to avoid globally clustering the heterogeneous Unknown category, and enforces margin-based repulsion emphasizing offline-mined hard negatives. On Google Speech Commands V2 under an event-level streaming protocol, MACR achieves > 40% relative FRR reduction over CE at strict points (0.5-0.2 FA/h) with minor changes in closed-set accuracy. As a training-only regularizer, MACR introduces zero additional parameters, MACs, or algorithmic latency to the deployed causal inference graph.

items.title: Mitigating Causality Mismatch with Causal Temporal Relation Distillation for Streaming Keyword Spotting
items.abstract: On-device keyword spotting (KWS) requires strictly causal models for zero-lookahead streaming. Distilling from non-causal teachers introduces causality mismatch: teacher features encode future context. Point-wise regression to these absolute features creates capacity conflicts that severely hinder continuous inference. To mitigate this, we propose Causal Temporal Relation Distillation, transferring intra-sample temporal topology instead of point-wise features. Applying a lower-triangular mask to relation matrices establishes a strictly realizable historical anchor. Our offline bidirectional variant (Ours-Bi) utilizes the teacher's full topology as an auxiliary prior without altering the zero-lookahead inference graph. On Google Speech Commands V2, Ours-Bi improves causal 1D-CNN accuracy from 95.12% to 96.91%. Under a continuous-stream protocol, it halves the False Rejection Rate (8.52% to 4.15% at 1.0 FA/h), demonstrating vastly superior long-context robustness.

items.title: Retention-Preserving Gradient Projection with Entropy-Guided Token-Level Distillation for Rehearsal-Free Continual ASR
items.abstract: Large-scale pretrained automatic speech recognition (ASR) models such as Whisper achieve strong generalization but suffer catastrophic forgetting under sequential domain adaptation. We propose a strict rehearsal-free continual learning method that uses distillation from the previous model to define a retention direction. We refine it with entropy-guided token-level distillation, up-weighting confident teacher tokens and down-weighting uncertain ones. When supervised and distillation gradients conflict, we apply retention-preserving gradient projection to attenuate the opposing supervised component with a tunable projection coefficient. Based on Fisher information, we freeze the encoder and adapt only the decoder. Compared with Learning without Forgetting (LwF), our method achieves a 7.2% relative reduction in mean word error rate (WER) after sequential adaptation to LibriSpeech, AMI, TED-LIUM, and SPGISpeech. It reduces the average multilingual degradation on Common Voice by 51.5%.

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Continual Learning for Automatic Speech Recognition
items.abstract: Speech foundation models enable strong general-purpose ASR and are attractive for downstream adaptation. However, their size and the catastrophic forgetting induced by sequential fine-tuning demand parameter-efficient and regularized training methods, motivating parameter-efficient continual learning (PECL). While PECL has been widely studied in NLP and vision, it has received less attention in ASR. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective PECL method based on recent advances in parameter-efficient fine-tuning for ASR. We partition pretrained weight matrices into head and tail subspaces according to singular values and restrict adaptation to approximate rotations within the low-energy tail subspace, preserving dominant components and reducing forgetting. For subsequent tasks, rotations are combined via weight averaging to further improve retention. Experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate reduced forgetting and superior overall performance compared to recent PECL baselines.

items.title: MoDiCoL: A Modular Diagnostic Continual Learning Dataset for Robust Speech Recognition
items.abstract: Modern Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems have made remarkable progress on standard benchmarks, yet performance gaps have emerged under real-world distribution shifts, caused by recording conditions, accents, speech impairments, and noise. Existing datasets and benchmarks typically isolate these factors, which overlooks their co-occurrence in real-world applications. In this paper, we argue that model robustness can be treated as a dynamic capability that continually develops, and we introduce MoDiCoL, a Modular Diagnostic Continual Learning dataset designed for controlled analysis of linguistic content, speaker characteristics, and acoustic environments. Furthermore, we propose a real-world-inspired continual learning curriculum to simulate incremental updates and study how robustness is acquired, transferred, and forgotten. We evaluate three continual learning strategies and provide detailed insights into robustness under evolving conditions.

items.title: SCOLoRA: Similarity Conditioned Signed Orthogonal LoRA for Continual Speaker Adaptation
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is expected to handle speaker and environmental variability, yet deployed systems encounter continual distribution shifts as new speakers arrive. Continual speaker adaptation personalizes one model along a speaker stream without revisiting past data, but sequential updates can cause catastrophic forgetting. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) offers a parameter efficient mechanism, and orthogonal low-rank adaptation (O-LoRA) reduces interference by separating update subspaces. However, enforcing task agnostic separation can suppress transfer among acoustically similar speakers. We introduce similarity conditioned signed orthogonal LoRA (SCOLoRA), which leverages speaker embedding similarity to dynamically balance subspace alignment and orthogonal separation via signed coefficients. Across ASR benchmarks, SCOLoRA consistently improves new speaker adaptation and reduces forgetting over LoRA-based continual learning baselines.

items.title: Mixture of Phonetic Experts Based Low-Rank Adaptation of Conformer Models for Accented English Speech Recognition
items.abstract: We present Mixture of Phonetic Experts based Low-Rank Adaptation (MoPE-LoRA), a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for accented English speech recognition. Recent mixture-of-experts approaches typically allocate experts per accent, implicitly treating accent identity as the primary axis of variation. In contrast, we organize adaptation along phonetic categories, motivated by the observation that accent differences are often expressed as systematic distortions of phoneme realization. MoPE-LoRA introduces a fixed set of six low-rank experts aligned with manner-of-articulation classes and performs frame-level routing through a hybrid mechanism that combines phoneme supervision with learned acoustic gating. Because the expert set is shared across accents, the model does not require accent-specific modules and naturally extends to previously unseen accents. Experiments on L2-ARCTIC show that MoPE-LoRA consistently improves over single LoRA and full fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation where one accent is held out during training, the proposed method yields a 12.3% relative improvement over single LoRA.
